AIE-1.chapter: Introduction to Building AI Applications with Foundation Models
AIE-1.about: This chapter explains why AI engineering grew so fast: big models are now sold as a service, so anyone can build on them. It then covers common use cases, how to plan an AI product, and how the AI engineering stack differs from classic ML engineering.
ideas: A demo is cheap and a product is not: the book says the last stretch of quality (for example 80% to 95%) can take several times longer than the first.
Decide the role of AI in your product early: critical or optional, reactive or proactive, and how much a human stays in the loop. These choices set the quality and speed you need.
Define success in business terms first (share of requests automated, time saved), then set a usefulness threshold for quality, latency and cost per request.
AI engineering is mostly about adapting and evaluating someone else's model, not training your own. Open-ended outputs make evaluation the hard part.
Start with prompt-based adaptation, which needs little data. Move to finetuning only when prompts are not enough.
Plan for maintenance: models, prices and rules change quickly, so you need versioning and evaluation in place before you swap a model.
AIE-1.read_when: Read it when you are deciding whether and how to build an AI feature, or when you need to explain to your team how this work differs from ordinary ML or back-end work.

sections.Three Layers of the AI Stack: Splits any AI application into three layers: application development (prompts, context, evaluation, interface), model development (training, finetuning, datasets, inference optimization) and infrastructure (serving, data and compute, monitoring). A builder usually starts at the top layer and goes down only when needed.
sections.AI Engineering Versus ML Engineering: Names three differences: you use a model someone else trained, so the work shifts to adapting it; models are bigger and slower, so efficiency matters more; and outputs are open-ended, which makes evaluation much harder. It also separates prompt-based adaptation, which leaves weights alone, from finetuning, which changes them.
sections.Planning AI Applications: Says a cool demo is easy and a profitable product is hard, so think before building. Start with why you build (a threat, a chance to gain, or fear of being late), whether to build or buy, and what moat protects you. It names technology, data and distribution as the three kinds of advantage.
sections.The role of AI and humans in the applica: Describes three design choices: AI is critical or complementary, features are reactive or proactive, and they update continually or periodically. It also introduces human-in-the-loop and the Crawl-Walk-Run path, where automation grows as the acceptance rate of AI suggestions proves itself.
sections.Setting Expectations: Tells you to define success as business impact first, such as the share of messages automated or labour saved. Then set a usefulness threshold across quality, latency (time to first token, time per output token, total), and cost per request, so a weak product is not shown to customers.
sections.Milestone Planning: Says to evaluate existing models first, because the stronger they are, the less you must build. Warns about the last-mile problem: a demo takes a weekend, but going from good to great takes months, and LinkedIn needed one month for 80% and four more for 95%. It also covers the upkeep burden from fast model, price and regulation changes.
sections.Conversational Bots: Lists chatbots as a versatile use case: customer support, product copilots that guide people through tasks, companions, voice assistants and smart game characters. For companies, support bots are the most popular because they answer faster and cut cost.
sections.Information Aggregation: Covers using AI to summarize and distill emails, documents and meetings, including the talk-to-your-docs pattern. One example is Instacart's internal prompt template that turns messy conversations into facts, open questions and action items.
sections.Data Organization: Explains that photos, videos, contracts and logs are unstructured, and AI can make them searchable by describing them or extracting structured fields. Examples run from reading receipts and licenses to pulling data out of contracts and reports.
sections.Workflow Automation: Presents automation of repetitive tasks such as invoicing, lead management and data entry as the end goal. Many tasks need outside tools, and AI that can plan and use tools is called an agent.

AIE-2.about: This chapter explains the design choices that make foundation models differ: training data, architecture and size, and post-training. It spends its second half on sampling, which is how a model turns probabilities into text, and on why that makes outputs inconsistent and sometimes false.
ideas: A model picks each next token by sampling from a probability distribution, so the same prompt can give different answers.
Temperature reshapes those probabilities. Low values give consistent but duller output, high values give varied but less coherent output, and 0 in practice means always pick the top token.
Generating several answers and choosing one (by highest average logprob, a verifier, a heuristic or majority vote) improves quality, but each extra answer costs about the same as the first.
To get structured output, you can prompt, post-process, retry, constrain sampling or finetune. The first three are light fixes, the last two are stronger.
Fixing temperature, top-p, top-k and seed reduces inconsistency but never guarantees it, because hardware can also change the result.
Hallucination has two proposed causes: the model treats its own earlier output as fact, and training teaches it to imitate answers that rely on knowledge it lacks.
AIE-2.read_when: Read the sampling part when your app gives different answers to the same input, returns broken JSON, or you need to decide how to set temperature and handle hallucination.

sections.Sampling Fundamentals: Explains that a language model first computes a probability for every token in its vocabulary, turning raw scores (logits) into probabilities with softmax. Always taking the top token (greedy sampling) works for classification but makes text dull, so models instead sample in proportion to the probabilities.
sections.Sampling Strategies: Covers the knobs that control sampling: temperature rescales scores to favour or flatten likely tokens, top-k and top-p limit which tokens are considered, and stopping conditions cap length. It also covers generating many answers and picking the best, and notes that logprobs are useful for debugging and classification but many providers expose them poorly.
sections.Structured Outputs: Says production apps often need output in a fixed format, either because the task is semantic parsing such as text-to-SQL or because another program consumes it. It ranks five ways to get it: prompting, post-processing, retrying, constrained sampling and finetuning. Note that a provider's JSON mode only promises valid JSON, not correct content, and cut-off output can still break parsing.
sections.The Probabilistic Nature of AI: States that because models sample, they are inconsistent (same input gives different outputs, or tiny input changes give very different ones) and they hallucinate. It suggests caching, fixed sampling settings and a fixed seed to reduce inconsistency, warns these never fully guarantee it, and presents two hypotheses for why hallucinations happen.

AIE-3.about: This chapter explains why evaluating open-ended AI output is hard and surveys the methods: exact checks (functional correctness, reference matching, similarity), AI as a judge, and comparative ranking. Its angle is to show how each method works and where it fails.
ideas: Functional correctness, meaning whether the output does its job (code passes tests, a booking succeeds), is the best metric when you can automate it.
Exact match only suits short, fixed answers. For longer text, lexical or semantic similarity to a reference works better, but needs good reference data.
An AI judge is fast, cheap and works without reference answers, but it is a model plus a prompt, so changing either one gives you a different judge.
Judge prompts should state the task, the criteria and the scoring system. Classification or a small 1 to 5 scale works better than wide numeric ranges, and examples help.
AI judges are inconsistent and biased: they favour their own answers, the first option, and longer answers. Do not trust a judge whose model and prompt you cannot see.
Add the cost of judging into your budget, and back it up with exact checks or human review.
AIE-3.read_when: Read it when you need to decide how to score your app's answers automatically, or when you want to know whether an LLM judge can be trusted.

sections.Exact Evaluation: Separates evaluation that gives an unambiguous result from subjective grading. It covers functional correctness (run the output and test it, as code benchmarks do with unit tests and the pass@k score) and comparison against reference data by exact match, lexical similarity (word and n-gram overlap, edit distance) and semantic similarity. It warns that exact match breaks on anything but short answers and that a good answer can score low if the references are poor.
sections.AI as a Judge: Describes using a model to grade another model's output, now one of the most common production methods because it is fast, cheap and needs no reference answers. It gives prompt advice (state the task, criteria and scoring system, prefer classification or small scales, add examples) and lists the weaknesses: inconsistency, unstandardized criteria, extra cost and latency, and biases such as self-preference, first-position and verbosity bias. It concludes judges should be paired with exact checks or human review.

AIE-4.about: This chapter shows how to use evaluation methods for your own application: choose criteria, pick a model, and build an evaluation pipeline. It also compares commercial APIs with self-hosted models and explains why public benchmarks cannot be fully trusted.
ideas: Define evaluation criteria before you build (evaluation-driven development). Group them into domain capability, generation quality, instruction following, and cost and latency.
Pick a model in four steps: drop models whose hard attributes do not fit, shortlist using public benchmarks, test with your own pipeline, then keep monitoring in production.
Weigh API versus self-hosting on seven axes: data privacy, data lineage, performance, functionality, cost, control, and on-device use.
Public benchmarks and leaderboards are only a shortlist tool, because they cover few capabilities and are often contaminated by test data in training sets.
Evaluate each component of the system as well as the end-to-end result, and write a scoring guideline with examples for good and bad answers.
Keep several evaluation sets (typical traffic, known failures, typos, out of scope inputs), and check that your set is large enough to give stable results.
AIE-4.read_when: Read it when you must choose between models or providers, or when you are designing the test set and scoring for your own AI feature.

sections.Evaluation Criteria: Argues that you should decide how you will evaluate an app before building it, and that evaluation is the biggest bottleneck to AI adoption. It sorts criteria into domain capability, generation capability (such as factual consistency and safety), instruction following, and cost and latency. It also covers how to measure each, for example checking factual consistency against given context with an AI judge.
sections.Model Selection Workflow: Splits model attributes into hard ones you cannot change (license, size, your privacy policy) and soft ones you can improve. Then it gives a four-step loop: filter by hard attributes, shortlist with public data, test with your own pipeline, and monitor in production. It notes the steps repeat as you learn more.
sections.Model Build Versus Buy: Compares commercial APIs with hosting an open model along seven axes: data privacy, data lineage, performance, functionality, cost, control, and on-device use. APIs are easier and usually strongest but cost per use and can change under you; self-hosting gives control and logprobs but needs engineering effort. It advises choosing a standard API shape so models are easy to swap.
sections.Navigate Public Benchmarks: Explains that benchmarks and leaderboards help shortlist models but have limits: leaderboards use few benchmarks, scores need weighting because scales differ, and data contamination (training on the test set) inflates results. Treat public scores as a way to pick a few models, then test them on your own data.
sections.Design Your Evaluation Pipeline: Gives a three-step recipe: evaluate every component and each turn and task, write a clear evaluation guideline with a scoring rubric tied to business metrics, and choose methods and annotated data. It suggests mixing cheap checks on all data with costly judges on a sample, slicing data into several test sets, checking the sample size with bootstrapping, and logging every evaluation variable.

AIE-5.about: This chapter covers how to write prompts that work and how to defend an application against prompt attacks. It treats prompt engineering as a real experimental practice that needs versioning and evaluation, not word fiddling.
ideas: Write clear, explicit instructions, give examples, state the output format, and give enough context. Prompt tricks that depend on one model's quirks age fast.
Split a complex task into smaller prompts chained together. This helps monitoring, debugging and parallel runs, and GoDaddy found it improved results and cut tokens.
Ask the model to reason step by step or to critique its own answer, but expect higher latency and cost.
Keep prompts out of code and version them, ideally in a catalog where each app can pin the version it uses.
Models use the start and end of a long prompt better than the middle. Test long prompts with a needle-in-a-haystack check.
Defend in layers (model, prompt, system), assume your system prompt will leak, and never let generated actions run unchecked. Risk can be reduced but not removed.
AIE-5.read_when: Read it when you are writing or reorganizing the prompts in your app, or when you need to threat-model prompt injection before giving a model tools or private data.

sections.System Prompt and User Prompt: Explains that the system prompt carries the developer's task description and the user prompt carries the task, but a model merges them into one prompt using its own chat template. A wrong template fails silently, so the advice is to follow the template exactly and print the final prompt before sending. A system prompt may help because it comes first or because the model was trained to favour it.
sections.Context Length and Context Efficiency: Notes that context limits have grown from about 1K tokens to millions, but models do not use all positions equally well: they handle the start and end of a prompt better than the middle. It recommends a needle-in-a-haystack test, with private data, to see how your model copes, and shortening prompts if quality drops as context grows.
sections.Prompt Engineering Best Practices: Collects techniques that work across models: write clear instructions, give a persona and examples, state the output format and end markers, supply enough context, split complex tasks into subtasks, and let the model think step by step. It also says to iterate, to version and test prompts against fixed data, and to evaluate each prompt within the whole system.
sections.Organize and Version Prompts: Recommends keeping prompts separate from code, which makes them reusable, testable, readable and open to subject-matter experts. It adds metadata such as model and sampling settings. Versioning prompts in git forces every app that shares a prompt onto the new version, so larger teams use a prompt catalog where each app picks a version.
sections.Defensive Prompt Engineering: Introduces the three kinds of prompt attack (prompt extraction, jailbreaking and injection, and information extraction) and the harm they can cause, from unauthorized tool or code execution and data leaks to brand damage. It frames the rest of the chapter as how each attack works and how to defend.
sections.Proprietary Prompts and Reverse Prompt E: Says teams guard their prompts, and attackers try to recover them by analysing outputs or tricking the model into repeating its instructions. Many supposedly leaked prompts are just model hallucinations. The advice is to write your system prompt as if it will become public, and it argues that prompts are a maintenance liability more than a moat.
sections.Jailbreaking and Prompt Injection: Defines jailbreaking as getting a model past its safety rules and prompt injection as smuggling instructions into user input, and says attacks work because models follow instructions. It describes manual tricks (obfuscation, format changes, roleplay), automated attacks, and indirect injection, where malicious text sits in a web page, email or database record that the model reads through a tool.
sections.Information Extraction: Describes attacks that pull out a model's training data or the private data in its context, for data theft, privacy violations or copyright copying. Models can memorize and regurgitate text, larger models more so, and a repeated-word prompt once made ChatGPT leak training text. Filters on personal data in requests and responses reduce the risk.
sections.Defenses Against Prompt Attacks: Recommends learning your weak points with red teaming and attack-test tools, and measuring both the violation rate and the false refusal rate. Defenses sit at three levels: model (an instruction hierarchy where tool output ranks lowest), prompt (explicit prohibitions, repeating the instruction after the input), and system (isolating code execution, human approval for impactful actions, input and output guardrails). It warns that risk can never be fully removed.

AIE-6.about: This chapter covers the two main ways to give a model the right context for each query: retrieval-augmented generation, and agents that use tools. It also covers memory, which helps both handle more information than fits in the context window.
ideas: A RAG system has a retriever and a generator, and its quality depends mostly on the retriever. Evaluate retrieval (context precision and recall), the final answers and the embeddings separately.

Term-based search (BM25) is fast, cheap and strong out of the box but misses meaning. Embedding search finds meaning but can blur exact terms such as error codes. Production systems often combine them.
Retrieval can be improved with sensible chunking (size, overlap), reranking, rewriting the query so it stands alone, and adding context or metadata to each chunk.
An agent is a model plus an environment and a set of tools, with read-only and write actions. Write actions need extra care and often human approval.
Agent errors compound: 95% accuracy per step falls to about 60% over 10 steps. Plan first, validate the plan, then execute, and reflect after steps.
Memory has three layers (internal knowledge, short-term context, long-term external storage), and a simple first-in-first-out policy can drop the most important early messages.
AIE-6.read_when: Read it when you are building a retrieval pipeline, choosing between keyword and vector search, or giving a model tools and need to know how agents plan and fail.

sections.RAG: Defines RAG as improving a model's answer by retrieving relevant information from external sources such as a database, past chats or the web. It argues that long context windows will not replace RAG: data keeps growing, models use long context poorly, and every extra token costs money and time. It treats context construction as the counterpart of feature engineering in classic ML.
sections.RAG Architecture: Describes a RAG system as a retriever (which indexes data and then queries it) plus a generator that answers from what was retrieved. Documents are split into chunks, the best chunks are joined with the user prompt, and the result goes to the model. The retriever's quality largely decides whether the system works.
sections.Embedding-based retrieval: Explains that embedding search ranks documents by meaning, not shared words: chunks are turned into vectors at index time, the query is embedded with the same model, and the k closest vectors are returned. Exact k-nearest-neighbour search is precise but slow, so large datasets use approximate methods such as LSH, HNSW, product quantization, IVF and Annoy.
sections.Term-based retrieval: Describes keyword retrieval, which ranks documents by how often a query term appears (term frequency) weighted by how rare the term is across documents (inverse document frequency). BM25 adjusts this for document length, runs on an inverted index in tools like Elasticsearch, and remains a strong baseline that is hard to beat.
sections.Comparing retrieval algorithms: Weighs the two approaches: term-based is faster, cheaper and good out of the box but hard to improve, while embedding-based can win after tuning but is costlier and can blur exact terms like error codes. It recommends measuring context precision and recall, ranking metrics and embedding quality, and notes that vector storage can cost a large share of model spending.
sections.Combining retrieval algorithms: Says production systems usually mix methods, called hybrid search. They can run in sequence (a cheap retriever fetches candidates, a more precise step reranks them) or in parallel, merging the ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, which sums a score of one over the rank (plus a constant) from each retriever.
sections.Retrieval Optimization: Introduces four tactics for getting the right documents back: chunking strategy, reranking, query rewriting and contextual retrieval. It also gives a checklist for evaluating a retrieval product, such as hybrid support, scalability, indexing time, query latency and pricing.
sections.Reranking: Says a second pass can reorder the retriever's first results to be more accurate, especially when you must cut how many documents go into the prompt. Results can also be reranked by recency for time-sensitive uses. In context reranking, exact position matters less than in search, though start and end positions still help.
sections.Query rewriting: Shows that a follow-up such as a bare name is ambiguous, so it should be rewritten into a standalone question before retrieval, either with heuristics or by prompting a model. If rewriting needs facts the system lacks, such as who someone's wife is, the model should say it cannot resolve the query instead of inventing an answer.
sections.Contextual retrieval: Recommends attaching context to each chunk so it is easier to find: keywords, tags, extracted entities such as an error code, questions the chunk answers, or a short model-written note placing the chunk within its source document (Anthropic's method). The augmented chunk is what gets indexed.
sections.Chunking strategy: Covers how to split documents: by fixed size in characters, words, sentences or paragraphs, or recursively by smaller units, with a small overlap so boundary information survives. Smaller chunks add variety but can lose context and mean more vectors to store and search. There is no universal best size, so test.
sections.RAG Beyond Texts: Extends RAG to other data. Multimodal RAG retrieves images or other media with captions or a shared multimodal embedding model such as CLIP. Tabular data needs a different flow: a model writes a SQL query from the question and table schemas, the query runs, and the result is used to write the answer.
sections.RAG with tabular data: Shows the flow for questions that need table data: text-to-SQL, SQL execution, then answer generation from the result. If there are too many tables to fit in the prompt, add a step that picks which tables are relevant first.
sections.Agents: Frames agents as the more general pattern: a model that can use tools to gather information and act, which makes RAG a special case. It warns that this section is more experimental than the rest of the book because there is no settled framework for building or evaluating agents.
sections.Agent Overview: Defines an agent as something that perceives an environment and acts on it, characterized by that environment and its tools. It notes that agents need stronger models because errors compound across steps (95% per step is about 60% over 10 steps) and because failures matter more once tools can change things.
sections.Tools: Groups tools into knowledge augmentation (retrievers, SQL, web browsing), capability extension (a calculator, a code interpreter, converters, captioning) and write actions that change the world. It stresses that write actions are risky and need trust and safeguards, and that more tools means more capability but harder use.
sections.Function calling: Explains how tool use works in APIs: you declare tools with a name, parameters and description, choose which are allowed per query (required, none or auto), and the model replies with the tool name and arguments for you to execute. Some APIs ensure the function is valid but cannot ensure the argument values are right, so log and inspect them.
sections.Planning: Describes planning as breaking a task into steps, and says to separate planning from execution so a plan is validated by simple rules or a model before it runs. It covers intent classification to choose tools, human involvement for risky steps, and doubts about whether language models plan well.
sections.Planning granularity: Describes the trade-off between detailed plans (harder to write, easier to run) and high-level ones. It suggests hierarchical planning and writing plans in natural language rather than exact function names, so tool changes do not break the planner, with a cheaper translator turning steps into calls.
sections.Complex plans: Lists control flows a plan can use (sequential, parallel, if, for loop) and notes that with agents the model decides them, which makes non-sequential plans harder. It also covers reflection and error correction, including the ReAct pattern of thought, action, observation and Reflexion, which are fairly easy to add and can help a lot but cost tokens and latency.
sections.Agent Failure Modes and Evaluation: Says to evaluate an agent by listing its failure modes and measuring each. Planning failures include invalid tools, bad parameters or values, missing constraints and wrongly claiming success; tool failures mean wrong tool output; efficiency covers steps, cost and time. Print every tool call and output so you can inspect them.
sections.Memory: Describes three kinds of memory: the model's internal knowledge, short-term memory (the context window) and long-term memory (external retrieval). Memory helps with overflow, keeping information across sessions, consistency and structured data. First-in-first-out trimming is simple but can lose the early messages that state the purpose, so summarising or reflecting on what to keep is often better.

AIE-7.about: This chapter explains when finetuning a model is worth the cost, how it compares with RAG, and why memory is its main bottleneck. It then covers memory-efficient methods, above all parameter-efficient finetuning and LoRA, plus model merging.
ideas: Finetuning is usually tried only after serious, systematic prompting experiments. Many cases where prompting seems not to work turn out to come from sloppy prompt tests.
Choose by failure type: if the model lacks or has outdated information, use RAG; if its behaviour is wrong (format, style, relevance), consider finetuning. The book sums this up as form versus facts.
If you have both kinds of problems, start with RAG, and start with simple keyword search before vector databases.
Finetuning for one task can make a model worse at others, and it brings ongoing costs: data, ML skill, serving, and a policy for when a newer base model replaces yours.
Full finetuning of a 7B model needs about 56 GB of memory with a common optimizer, which is why parameter-efficient methods are popular.
LoRA trains two small matrices that are merged back into the original weights, so it adds almost no inference latency and needs far fewer trainable parameters.
AIE-7.read_when: Read it when someone on your team proposes finetuning and you need to decide whether RAG or better prompts would do, or when you want to understand what LoRA is.

sections.When to Finetune: Says finetuning needs far more than prompting does (data, hardware and ML talent), so it is normally attempted after extensive prompt experiments. The two are not exclusive, and real systems often use both.
sections.Reasons to Finetune: Lists the main reasons: improving quality on your specific task or data format, such as an uncommon SQL dialect, enforcing structured outputs like JSON or YAML, and reducing bias with curated data. Small finetuned models can beat much larger general ones on a narrow task, and distillation trains a small model on a large model's outputs.
sections.Reasons Not to Finetune: Warns that finetuning for one task can hurt others, needs costly data and training skill, requires you to serve and maintain the model, and can be overtaken by new base models. It says to start with prompting, noting that complaints about prompting often come from minimal, unsystematic tests, and that general models can beat domain-specific ones such as BloombergGPT.
sections.Finetuning and RAG: Separates information-based failures (missing or outdated facts), which RAG fixes, from behaviour-based failures (wrong format, style or relevance), which finetuning can fix. One study found RAG on a base model beat finetuned models on current-events questions. With both problems, start with RAG, using simple term-based retrieval first, and combine the two later if needed.
sections.Finetuning Techniques: Introduces memory-efficient ways to adapt models, centred on parameter-efficient finetuning, and also model merging, an experimental way to combine several models. The reason is that memory cost limits who can finetune large models.
sections.Parameter-Efficient Finetuning: Contrasts full finetuning, where every weight is trained and a 7B model needs about 56 GB of memory, with partial finetuning, which saves memory but needs many parameters to match quality. PEFT adds a small number of trainable parameters (for example adapters) and reaches near-full quality with a few percent of them, and with fewer examples. The first adapters add some inference latency.
sections.LoRA: Explains LoRA as splitting a weight update into two small matrices of a chosen rank, training only those, and merging the result back into the original weights, so there is no extra inference latency. It reports comparable or better results than full finetuning on GPT-3 with a tiny fraction of the parameters, and suggests it works because pre-trained models have a low intrinsic dimension.

AIE-8.about: This chapter argues that model quality depends on training data quality, and walks through curating data, synthesizing it with AI, and processing it. It focuses on data for finetuning, which matters most to application developers.
ideas: Think of data in three dimensions: quality, coverage (diversity) and quantity. The amount you need depends on the finetuning method, the task's difficulty and how good the base model already is.
Different training goals need different data shapes: instruction and response pairs, preference triples (winning and losing answer), or sequences for self-supervised training.
AI-generated data can add quantity, fill coverage gaps and sometimes beat human quality, but it needs verification, and training on unfiltered model output can degrade a model.
Model distillation trains a small student model on a larger teacher's outputs. It can give a much cheaper model for deployment, but some licenses forbid using outputs to train other models.
Processing matters as much as collection: inspect the data, remove duplicates and fix the format before training.
AIE-8.read_when: Read it when you plan to finetune or distill a model and need to know how much data, of what kind, and how to generate and check it.

sections.Model Distillation: Describes distillation as training a small student model to imitate a large teacher, usually on data the teacher generated, to get a smaller and faster model that keeps most of the quality (DistilBERT, Alpaca and BuzzFeed's cheaper model are examples). It adds that licenses may forbid using a model's outputs to train others, that synthetic data is not always distillation, and that training on unverified self-generated data can hurt.

AIE-9.about: This chapter is about making model serving faster and cheaper. It defines the metrics to track, explains the hardware and model-level bottlenecks, and covers techniques at the model level (compression, faster decoding) and the service level (batching, prompt caching).
ideas: Total latency is roughly time to first token plus time per output token times the number of output tokens. Users judge the first token and the pace separately.
Look at latency percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99) rather than the average, because a few slow requests skew the mean.
Throughput and cost trade off against latency. Goodput, which counts only requests that meet your latency targets, shows what users really get.
GPU utilization from standard tools can be misleading. Model FLOP/s utilization and bandwidth utilization show how efficiently the hardware is really used.
Prompt caching reuses repeated prompt prefixes such as a long system prompt, and can cut cost and time to first token a lot (the book cites savings of up to 90% cost with one provider).
Streaming responses and batch APIs suit different needs: streaming lowers the wait for the first token, batch APIs suit work that is not urgent.
AIE-9.read_when: Read it when your app feels slow or the model bill is too high, and you want to know which metrics to measure and what levers exist, even if you only use a hosted API.

sections.Inference Performance Metrics: Defines the metrics to measure. Latency splits into time to first token and time per output token, so total latency is the first plus the second times the output length, and it should be read as percentiles rather than an average. It also covers throughput (output tokens per second, which drives cost), goodput (requests that meet your latency targets), and utilization measures such as model FLOP/s and bandwidth utilization, warning that plain GPU utilization can mislead.

AIE-10.chapter: AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback
AIE-10.about: This chapter assembles the book's techniques into one application architecture, starting from a bare model call and adding context, guardrails, routing, caching and agent patterns step by step. It then covers monitoring, orchestration and how to collect and use user feedback.
ideas: Start with the simplest design (query in, model answer out) and add a component only when a problem calls for it: context, guardrails, router and gateway, caches, then agent patterns.

Guard both sides. Input guardrails stop private data leaking to external APIs and block attacks; output guardrails catch bad formats, hallucinations and unsafe content, often with a simple retry or a handoff to a human.

A router (an intent classifier) sends each query to the right model or workflow and can reject out-of-scope requests cheaply. A gateway gives one safe entry point to many models, with access control, cost limits and fallbacks.
Exact caching is simple but must never cache answers that depend on one user. Semantic caching is riskier because a wrong similarity match returns a wrong answer.
Design observability in from the start: log every configuration, prompt, tool call and output, link events into traces, and watch for drift in prompts, user behaviour and the provider's model.
Conversation gives rich implicit feedback (stopping early, rephrasing, regenerating, edits). Treat it as user data and respect privacy.
AIE-10.read_when: Read it when you are drawing the whole architecture of an AI application, or deciding what to log, cache, guard and measure before going to production.

sections.AI Engineering Architecture: Presents a general architecture built up in steps from the simplest form, a query sent to a model. It adds context construction, guardrails, a router and gateway, caching, and agent patterns, with monitoring and orchestration around them. It says to add components in the order your own needs dictate.
sections.Step 1. Enhance Context: Says the first expansion is usually giving the model per-query context through retrieval and tools (web, news, weather and other APIs), likening it to feature engineering. Providers support this to different degrees, for example in upload limits and parallel tool execution, so compare them with your needs.

sections.Step 2. Put in Guardrails: Introduces guardrails as protection placed wherever the system is exposed to risk, split into input and output guardrails. Risk can be reduced but never fully removed.
sections.Put in Guardrails: Introduces guardrails as protection placed wherever the system is exposed to risk, split into input and output guardrails. Risk can be reduced but never fully removed.
sections.Input guardrails: Explains that input guardrails guard against leaking private data to external APIs and against malicious prompts. Sensitive data detectors can block a query or mask items such as phone numbers with placeholders, and a reverse map restores them in the answer.
sections.Output guardrails: Says output guardrails catch failures (empty or malformatted responses, hallucinations, toxic or private content) and define what to do next. Simple retries often work, optionally in parallel to save time at higher cost, and some cases are handed to humans, for example when sentiment turns angry. It also asks you to track false refusals.
sections.Guardrail implementation: Notes the trade-offs: guardrails add latency, and output checks work badly with streaming because unsafe text may reach users before it is blocked. How many you need depends on whether you self-host or use an API, and ready-made options exist, though providers must balance safety against flexibility.
sections.Step 3. Add Model Router and Gateway: Describes a router, usually an intent classifier, that sends queries to specialized or cheaper models, declines out-of-scope requests and asks for clarification on ambiguous ones. It also describes a gateway, a unified secure layer in front of all models that centralizes keys, access control, cost limits, fallbacks, logging and sometimes caching.

sections.Step 4. Reduce Latency with Caches: Covers system caching, as distinct from the inference caches in Chapter 9. Exact caching reuses results for identical requests and needs an eviction policy; it should skip user-specific or time-sensitive queries and can leak data if an answer containing one user's information is cached. Semantic caching matches similar queries by embedding, but depends on embeddings, a threshold and vector search, so its value is doubtful unless hit rates are high.

sections.Step 5. Add Agent Patterns: Says the last step is letting the flow loop back, such as retrieving more after judging an answer incomplete, and allowing write actions like sending email or placing orders. Write actions add capability and risk, and a more complex system has more failure points and is harder to debug.

sections.Monitoring and Observability: Argues that observability should be designed in, not added later. It rates observability by time to detect, time to respond and change failure rate, and says to design metrics around the failures you fear: format errors, factual consistency, safety, length and cost, latency per user, and user signals. Metrics should be sliceable by user, release and prompt version.
sections.Logs and traces: Explains that metrics show something went wrong while logs show what happened, so log everything: configuration, sampling settings, prompt template, user query, final prompt, outputs, tool calls and tool outputs, with IDs. Traces link these events into the full path of one request with timing and cost, so a failure can be pinned to a step. It adds drift detection for prompt, user behaviour and model changes.
sections.AI Pipeline Orchestration: Describes an orchestrator as the tool that defines the components (models, data sources, tools) and chains them from query to answer, passing data between steps and flagging breaks. It recommends starting without one, since an orchestrator can hide details and add latency, and judging tools by integration, support for complex pipelines, and ease of use and scale.
sections.User Feedback: Treats feedback as both an evaluation signal and proprietary training data, to be handled with privacy care. It separates explicit feedback (ratings, thumbs) from implicit feedback, and lists conversational signals such as early termination, corrections and rephrasing, complaints, regeneration, edits and conversation length. It also covers when and how to ask for feedback, and its limits.
